title: Malik and Ahmad
hook: the Muwatta of Malik and the Musnad of Ahmad, early and vast
tomorrow: The four books of the Shia

segments.voice: Yesterday: the four Sunan, which with the two Sahihs make up the six books.

Medina. A teacher sits in the city where the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ lived and was buried, with students gathered around him and a book he has written. Tradition says he kept working on it, revising and trimming, for a long time before he was satisfied. He called it al-Muwatta: the trodden path, the way made smooth by the people who walked it before. His name was Malik ibn Anas. Today, two collections that stand beside the six books and are counted among the early ones. Malik and Ahmad.
screen: `A TEACHER IN MEDINA.` → `THE TRODDEN PATH.` → `BESIDE THE SIX BOOKS.`

segments.voice: First, the Muwatta. It's arranged by topics of law, like the Sunan, but it holds more than the Prophet's words. Next to them, Malik records what Companions did, what the people of Medina practiced, and his own judgment on the question. For Malik, the way the city of the Prophet actually lived was itself a kind of witness. One short report from it is easy to carry: the Prophet said that he was sent to perfect good character. Second, a line of teachers. Tradition says al-Shafi'i studied the Muwatta with Malik, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal later studied with al-Shafi'i. Founders of schools of law, each one sitting in front of the one before. Third, the Musnad. Ahmad's book is vast, and built a completely different way. Musnad means supported, propped up by a chain. Instead of chapters on prayer or trade, it's arranged by Companion: all the reports that came through one Companion, then all through the next. Want what Abu Bakr narrated? It's together. Want everything about prayer? You'll have to hunt through the whole book. Ahmad wasn't building a handbook. He was building an archive. Fourth, the people behind the books. Tradition remembers both men holding firm when rulers of their day pressed them to say or do what they believed was wrong, and both paid for it. A collection is never only paper. It's a life spent listening, and sometimes a life spent refusing.
screen: `THE MUWATTA: HADITH AND MEDINA'S PRACTICE.` · `MALIK, AL-SHAFI'I, AHMAD.` · `THE MUSNAD: ARRANGED BY COMPANION.` · `A LIFE SPENT LISTENING.`

segments.voice: Say the Muwatta's line slowly, in three pieces: sent, to perfect, good character. Notice what it doesn't say: not sent to win arguments, not sent to be admired. All the care of these weeks, the biographies, the journeys, the fakes exposed, was for lines like this one, so bring to mind one moment this week when your own character slipped, and one when it held, and look at both without a verdict.
Malik and Ahmad. The Muwatta, the trodden path of Medina, and the Musnad, the reports arranged by the Companion who told them. Today's word.
Your line: early collections. Two more shelves that stand beside the six books. That's the week.

chat.says: If I want every hadith about prayer in one place, should I open Ahmad's Musnad?
options: It's hard there: the Musnad is arranged by Companion, not by topics like prayer.
Yes, the Musnad is the one sorted by topic, with a chapter just on prayer.
No, the Musnad holds only Medina's practice, with no hadith of the Prophet.
chat.meaning: Musnad means supported by a chain. Ahmad arranged it by Companion, so a topic like prayer is spread through the whole book.

al-Muwatta.meaning: Malik's book: the trodden path, the way made smooth

Musnad.meaning: a collection arranged by the Companion who narrated

Malik ibn Anas.meaning: the Medina teacher who wrote the Muwatta

al-Shafi'i.meaning: founder of a school of law, a student of Malik

Ahmad ibn Hanbal.meaning: compiler of the Musnad, a student of al-Shafi'i
